builder_plan.scenario: A self-hosted assistant is too expensive because its model uses most of the GPU memory.
builder_plan.change: Try the paper's supported lower-precision weights on a copy of your serving setup.
builder_plan.baseline: The same model at its original precision, on the same GPU.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Peak memory, task pass rate, latency, and total serving cost at the same context and load.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: TileQuant: Tile as the Precision-Allocation Unit for LLM Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization
summary: TileQuant replaces uniform-weight PTQ and column-wise mixed-precision retention with precision assignment at hardware-aligned 2D tiles, keeping only the highest-sensitivity tiles at 16-bit and quantizing the rest to 8-bit using offline calibration and a custom kernel. It costs an offline calibration and weight-reconstruction pass, a nonstandard kernel and buffer layout to integrate and maintain, and partial (16-bit) storage for retained tiles, so compression is below pure 8-bit. It can fail if calibration statistics do not transfer to production data, if the custom kernel underperforms or lacks support on the reader's specific GPU, or if retained-tile budgets are mis-set, degrading quality without recovery at runtime.
rationale: The method is training-free and targets a single GPU with 8/16-bit computation, which fits constrained infrastructure, but the gain depends on a custom kernel and calibration quality that require workload-specific validation before production adoption.

It costs an offline calibration and weight-reconstruction pass, a nonstandard kernel and buffer layout to integrate and maintain, and partial (16-bit) storage for retained tiles, so compression is below pure 8-bit. It can fail if calibration statistics do not transfer to production data, if the custom kernel underperforms or lacks support on the reader's specific GPU, or if retained-tile budgets are mis-set, degrading quality without recovery at runtime.
TileQuant reaches 2.66x the original model's generation throughput.
